I've tried asking teachers and students why they do what they do for eight hours every day, and if it's time effectively spent. Many of the reasons given are: to help children prepare for future jobs, to encourage interaction/socialization between kids, and to teach children the importance of civic duty and the humanities.

But I would say that public schools perform badly with all of those tasks. For example, if the purpose is to prepare kids for jobs, why are programming classes absent at most schools while unimportant classes like art and history are still mandatory? If the purpose is socialization, why are most schools structured in a one hour period of instruction and only five minutes of socialization? If the purpose is to teach civic duty and the humanities, why is eight hours a day necessary?

The public school system has remained largely unchanged for a century amidst a drastic change in how the world operates. When the assumed purpose is an exchange of information to a student, are teachers really necessary, what about schools? There is a huge array of free educational opportunities such as videos and books available on the internet that are vastly superior, in my opinion, to a teacher in terms of quality and efficiency.

What is the purpose of school? Are we achieving that goal? What can be done to fix this broken system? Do we really need centralized education institution anymore?

I've also submitted this to v/politics, feel free to join either thread.
[Discussion] What is the purpose of public education in the US? What can be done to fix it?

The purpose at its very core is to create a fundamentally equipped student body so that they can transition into the 'real world.' In recent years we are seeing more short comings some of this could be resolved by the removal of tenure, but that doesn't resolve the issue of a worse core curriculum. There should be more trade skills taught in school regarding very basic things like changing oil, replacing a hard drive, driving a nail properly, and mending garments or even how to garden. Other stuff like basic finance and how credit work and how to do your own taxes.

As a father now my four year old has a reading ability fat beyond what I had at that level thanks to certain games and even subtitles of all things. You could almost automate the process for the first few years but critical thinking skills require proper debate and discussion.

The role of the teacher should be self defined as someone to teach but not from a fixed texted or curriculum for anything other than a guideline for what to cover with text books serving as supplemental reading. I had several teachers in high school where the book was mostly irrelevant and only used as further reading or to cement what had been taught when away from school and my notes being the main key to knowing what would be tested and passing said test. My favorite and what I believe to be my best teacher used the classroom as a mixture of lecture and open discussion of the material. Since testing is really only a rudimentary way of establishing what's know she was able to get a better idea through debate and discussion and let us form our own opinions and debate the issues at hand. Now with this being a history class it allowed for this where as with a strict math or science class there would be more lecture and less discussion but it still should come back and involve greater class participation again so the teacher can gage modestly what the class really knew and didn't know.

My gripe with tenure is teaching should be every bit as competitive as any other field, but the down side is students need to be able to bond with their teacher so they can be quicker to get on board with what they're trying to teach them and sometimes they need time to establish themselves for this to occur, but being in a position for four years doesn't always mean someone is good at what they do only that they were able to meet the minimum criteria.

By the time a student graduates they should be at least qualified enough to get a bottom line factory job and survive. I took a test called Work Keys about a year ago and a lot of it I considered basic stuff but to some it was thought to be difficult. It covered things like troubleshooting a hydrolic lift and discerning where the malfunction was and other stuff such as calculating the resistance in a series of circuits or examine a diagram and either deriving certain information from it like where X or Y is or where if A event is occurring what precautions could be taken to prevent it or stop it. This test wasn't difficult and covered material I had done in high school but most still considered it a hard test and that's just sad.

Now that HOTS has been officially out for almost a month (most of us have probably played a lot longer, though) what are some of your favorites heroes?

Although he's pretty situational, Azmodan takes the cake for me. A unique kit with unique playstyle, and can be a decent overall contributor to the team if played correctly, even in team fights where he is traditionally at his weakest. And he's pretty efficient split-pushing if left alone (but not quite as good as Sylv or Zagara). He's even better if you queue with a friend to help get Orb stacks.

I think the trick to playing Azmo in team fights, which isn't obvious right away compared to some other heroes, is proper positioning and using abilities defensively, especially laser. I always try to keep my squishies within the radius of laser, so I can zone out melee assassins. Either the other team uses a CC on you to stop laser, or you melt your target, especially at 10 when you get black pool, and then March of Sin.

The best part, though? Dunking the enemy Nazeebo as he tries to sprint away from a losing team fight.

Honestly I would probably play Azmodunk all the time if dailies didn't get in the way.

I love the vikings. You need to be really concentrated to play them well. There is always the decision whether to split them up or group them, without awareness of what happens on the whole map your splitted vikings just die.

Sometimes it is hard to play with randoms, who do not understand that they can freely take camps and roam while your vikings soak xp, but often your enemies do not know how to play against the vikings as well. Most are surprised how much damage a spin can do when you are stacked up - and even more surprised that they can not flee because you are body blocking them.

Knowing when to use your boat really can make or break a teamfight. Jumping to evade enemies ults is incredibly fun and chasing the last survivor down with erik is always accomplishing. Of course its great to outvalue everyone, too!

TLV are definitely on my list of heroes to try during a free week.

What do you think about the TLV rework from the latest patch? Initial consensus elsewhere is 'they're broken' but since no one really likes change in general I tend to take such comments with a grain of salt.

They are way too squishy now. It seems they are now a proper specialist who can push lanes effectively and take camps, like Gazlowe does - but I doubt most people think its fun to just PvE all the time. At least with "Nordic attack squad" at level 13 they are still able to duel most heroes.
The main problem is, that they just feel like a completely new hero now, who fears teamfights. For example: A verdant sphered flamestrike at level 20 with 15% abilitypower does around 1720 dmg, while Erik has only 1750 health. Before the patch you could just jump over that flamestrike, now you need to sacrifice your main damage source almost everytime to do so.
To sum this up: Getting all the defensive talents make them feel useless, while taking offensive talents makes for a fun, but not viable build.
I still do not think they will drop under 50% winrate, because of their xp soak.

How difficult is it to keep track of TLV? I really like seeing the insane micromanaging plays but I feel like managing 3 heroes while looking at the minimap and playing the field would be too overwhelming.

You definitely need sound enabled to play with them, as the warning sound makes a huge difference.
The awesome thing about them is, that they are always challenging. Every single game gives you the feeling, that one could have done better. That is what keeps you motivated to play them, the progress in your abilities is palpable. Do not be too afraid, just keep learning by doing.
